title: Training data and bias: why AI is not neutral
subtitle: AI learns from real data. That data contains human patterns.

sections.title: How a model learns and why data matters
sections.content:
A model learns patterns from an assembled training mixture. Depending on the system, that mixture may include publicly available text, licensed data, human-created examples, or synthetic data. It is not a complete or neutral representation of the world.

Suppose occupations are associated with men more often than women in the training examples. A model may reproduce that association and choose male forms more often in an open-ended task. The effect depends not only on data, but also on selection, labels, training objectives, model version, and later system instructions.

Research on machine translation has documented gendered assignments when the source text is ambiguous. Research on image datasets has also shown that unequal representation of regions and living contexts can contribute to different error rates. The actual effect must be measured for the particular model, task, and affected groups.

Bias is therefore not one defect with one cause. Data distribution, product decisions, and deployment context can combine to create systematic differences.
sections.keyTakeaway: Systematic bias can arise from data, labels, training objectives, product design, and deployment context. Test the actual system on relevant cases.

sections.title: What you can do
sections.content:
Bias cannot be assessed with one example prompt. A job advertisement can still serve as an initial observation exercise: generate several variants with controlled changes, then compare pronouns, requirements, tone, and omitted groups. Record the model, date, input, and output.

Use three checks in practice.

First: when text describes people or groups, compare its attributes, pronouns, and unstated assumptions with the intended purpose.

Second: for recommendations or classifications, compare relevant groups and error types with suitable test data. One plausible example is not evidence of consistent behavior.

Third: decisions affecting people need a named accountable person, a correction route, and checks against the applicable legal and professional requirements. "Human judgment" by itself is not a control procedure.

Record what was tested, the limits of the test, and who responds to a problem.
sections.keyTakeaway: Assess bias with controlled cases, suitable measures, and clear accountability. Individual examples provide signals, not proof.
